doc.title: TerraPulse · Furnas reservoir seen by NISAR
nav.switch.label: Ler em português
hero.kicker: Furnas reservoir · Minas Gerais, Brazil · June to October 2026
hero.title: On calm days, a radar satellite measured Furnas reservoir to within {mae_pct}%.
hero.dek: NISAR, the NASA–ISRO radar satellite, passed over Furnas {n} times between {d0} and {d1}. We measured the lake's water area on every pass and checked each number against the official water level reported by ANA, Brazil's national water agency.
hero.caption: NISAR HH backscatter, {d0}. Dark means almost no signal came back.
see.title: Water is the darkest thing on the map
see.p1: NISAR sends microwave pulses with a 24 cm wavelength (L-band) sideways toward the ground and records how much comes back. It works at night and through cloud.
see.p2: Calm water works like a mirror. The pulse bounces away from the satellite and almost nothing returns, so the lake shows up near black.
see.p3: Fields, forest and towns are rough. They scatter part of the pulse back to the antenna and show up in colour.
see.legend: Hover a class to find it on the map
see.l.water.d: almost no return in either channel
see.l.volume.d: likely tree cover or tall crops
see.l.field: Brighter in HH than in HV
see.l.note: A reading aid for one date ({d0}), not a land-cover map. Water is our official mask; the HV class is any pixel above {hv} dB.
see.probe: Move over the map to read the signal
see.cap: NISAR colour composite, {d0}. Red = HH, green = HV, blue = HH minus HV.
time.title: Same orbit, same angle, every 12 days
time.p1: NISAR repeats its ground track every 12 days. Track 024 crossed Furnas heading south at about 21:15 UTC on nine dates. There is no image for 2 August.
time.p2: Blue is what our method counts as water: radar signal in HH below {limiar} dB, inside ANA's official reservoir outline, ignoring patches under {mancha} km². The same threshold applies to every date.
time.p3: Two dates are flagged. On {w1} and {w2} the water returned {b1} and {b2} dB, against an average of {bcalm} dB on the calm dates. Wind roughening the surface would do that, but we have no wind data to confirm it. Both dates stay in the series, marked.
cmp.title: {d0s} against {d1s}
cmp.p1: Drag the handle. Left: {d0}. Right: {d1}. The thin line is ANA's official outline at the maximum normal level, {maxnormal} m.
cmp.p2: Turn on the change layer. Ochre pixels were water on {d0} and not on {d1}; light blue pixels are the reverse. Net change measured by NISAR: {net} km². The ANA level predicts {netexp} km². Switching it on also zooms to the 8 km window where the most water was lost.
cmp.caveat: The method's noise is about {ruido} km² per date. Read the pattern along the shores, not single pixels.
proof.title: The radar against the official water level
proof.p1: ANA publishes Furnas's water level every day. ANA's own level-to-area curve turns each level into the area the lake should cover. That gives an independent expected area for every NISAR pass.
proof.s1.l: mean error on the {ncalm} calm dates, or {mae_km2} km² on a lake of about {areatyp} km²
proof.s2.l: area change per metre of water level, measured by NISAR. ANA's curve gives {slopeana} km²/m
proof.s3.l: level drop, from {cmax} m on {dmax} to {cmin} m on {dmin}. That is about {varexp} km² of expected area
proof.c1.title: Water area on each pass, km²
proof.c2.title: Area against water level
proof.honest: What this shows, and what it doesn't. The radar confirmed that Furnas stayed stable through the 2026 dry season and caught the direction of the drawdown. The whole season moved the lake by about {varexp} km², only about three times the method's noise of {ruido} km². Changes smaller than that between two passes are not resolved; for those, the gauge is still the better instrument.
pol.title: One pass, three ways to look
pol.hh: HH: sent horizontal, received horizontal. The cleanest split between water and land. Our water mask uses only this channel.
pol.hv: HV: sent horizontal, received vertical. Only surfaces that scramble the wave send it back, such as tree crowns and tall crops. Water and bare ground stay dark.
pol.cor: Colour: red = HH, green = HV, blue = HH minus HV. Yellow-green areas return strongly in both channels. Purple areas are much brighter in HH than in HV.
hum.title: A power plant sets the level, not only the rain
hum.p1: Furnas is a hydroelectric reservoir. Its level rises and falls with how much water the plant lets through its turbines. Those releases follow rules from ANA and dispatch orders from ONS, the operator of Brazil's national grid.
hum.p2: This season the level moved between {cmin} and {cmax} m. Useful storage went from {vmax}% on {dvmax} to {vmin}% on {dvmin}, and was back at {vlast}% on {dlast}.
hum.p3: The outline on our maps marks the maximum normal level, {maxnormal} m. The lake stayed {gapmin} to {gapmax} m below it all season. A ring of shore that would be underwater at full level stayed dry.
hum.m: Area and level fell together from July to early September, then recovered in October.
hum.c: Releases for power generation exceeding the dry-season inflow, then the first rains of the wet season.
hum.e: ANA/ONS daily level bulletins for the nine pass dates.
hum.n: Inflow, outflow and rainfall. The cause above is a hypothesis, not a finding.
hum.g.title: Water level, m (ANA)
lim.title: What could be wrong
lim.1: These are NISAR's provisional GCOV products ({col}). Calibration may shift in later validated releases.
lim.2: All nine passes come from track 024, descending, frame 099. Other tracks would add dates and view angles.
lim.3: Wind roughens water and makes it brighter. On {wworst} the area came out {worst} km² below the expected value without a matching level change.
lim.4: Funil reservoir was planned as a stable control, but only {funil}% of it falls inside valid data on this track. It was left out.
lim.5: Smooth exposed soil can look as dark as water. Counting only inside ANA's outline limits this, but it may explain the {dexc} excess of {exc} km².
reuse.title: Three inputs, two commands
reuse.i1: from one track and frame, downloaded from ASF DAAC with a free NASA Earthdata login.
reuse.i2: as a shapefile or File Geodatabase. In Brazil, ANA/SNIRH publishes one per dam.
reuse.i3: to validate the result. Without them you still get the area series, unchecked.
